sources.citation: Bernhardt, Julia. 2019. A comparative study of the Northern Naga languages and their genetic classification. CanIL Electronic Working Papers 5: 1-23.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent. Lexicostatistic comparison of 15 wordlists (462 items, LSDO data) from seven Myanmar Northern Naga languages including one Lao [nlq] list; p. 13: 'The focus was limited to lexical similarity based on segmental phonology, excluding morphosyntactic and other phonological features, such as tone and syllable structure.' tone.quote: From these data, it can be concluded that each of the tone systems found in Patkaian varieties today are from the most part derived from common features of syllable structure and what was most likely a phonation distinction as described in van Dam (2018), but not onset voicing. The major exception to this are Gongvangpounyiu and Khiamniungan varieties, which also rely on the reconstructed phonation distinctions as the original features of what has become tone, but importantly also involved aspiration and onset voicing in a way that is not seen elsewhere in Patkaian varieties.
tone.summary: Branch-wide study of how tone arose in Patkaian (Northern Naga) languages; describes tone for Tangsa-Nocte, Wancho, Khiamniungan and Makyam, but never mentions Lao Naga or gives it a tone inventory.
tone.says: Branch-wide study of how tone arose in Patkaian (Northern Naga) languages; describes tone for Tangsa-Nocte, Wancho, Khiamniungan and Makyam, but never mentions Lao Naga or gives it a tone inventory.
